title: XOR: every pair cancels out
sub: Missing Number and Single Number III: a ^ a = 0, sum versus XOR, and the lowest 1 bit x & −x
cards/0/body:
a ^ b has a 1 wherever the bits differ. Three properties follow: a ^ a = 0, a ^ 0 = a, and order does not matter — XOR is commutative and associative. So the XOR of a collection of numbers is the XOR of those that occur an odd number of times: every pair cancels itself out, wherever its two halves sit.

Single Number (LeetCode #136): every number occurs twice, one occurs once. The XOR of the whole array is the answer: O(n) time, O(1) memory, no dictionary.

One more consequence: a ^ b = c ⇔ a ^ c = b. XOR is its own inverse — to “undo” a number, XOR it in once more. Missing Number, position hashing in games and Maximum XOR from the last lesson of this unit all rely on this.
cards/1/q: Every number occurs exactly three times, except one that occurs once. What does the XOR of the whole array give?
cards/1/options/0: The single number: the triples cancel themselves out
cards/1/options/1: The XOR of the single number and all the tripled numbers: each triple leaves one copy
cards/1/explain: Only pairs cancel: a ^ a ^ a = (a ^ a) ^ a = a. What is left is everything that occurs an odd number of times — the single number and one copy of each tripled number. This problem (Single Number II, #137) needs a different count, bit by bit; it is on the variations card.
cards/1/wrong/0: A triple is a pair plus one more copy: the pair cancels, the copy stays.
cards/1/wrong/2: Only a collection where every number occurs an even number of times folds down to zero.
cards/2/body:
Missing Number (#268): nums holds n distinct numbers from 0..n, one is missing — find it. n ≤ 10⁴; you want O(n) time and O(1) memory. Sorting is O(n log n), a HashSet is O(n) memory, and placing values at their indices, as in the hash table unit, destroys the input.

Sum: 0 + 1 + … + n minus the sum of the array. XOR: put the indices 0..n − 1 next to the values. Every number that is present shows up twice — as an index and as a value — and cancels. The missing one only shows up as an index and stays. Index n has no slot in the array, so the XOR starts at n.

The sum’s trap is overflow. The formula n * (n + 1) / 2 in int breaks at n ≥ 46,341: the product exceeds int.MaxValue, wraps around, and halving it ruins the result. Compute it in long. XOR has no carries, so there is nothing to overflow.
cards/3/q: n = 50,000. The array sum is computed correctly, and the expected one like this: int expected = n * (n + 1) / 2. What happens?
cards/3/options/0: The right answer: the overflow cancels out in the subtraction
cards/3/options/1: A wrong answer: n · (n + 1) = 2,500,050,000 does not fit in an int and wraps before the division
cards/3/explain: int.MaxValue = 2,147,483,647, and the product is 2,500,050,000. It wraps to −1,794,917,296, after the division that is −897,458,648 instead of 1,250,025,000, and the answer is garbage. The fix is (long)n * (n + 1) / 2, or XOR.
cards/3/wrong/0: It would cancel if only additions and subtractions followed: in int they work modulo 2³², and a final result that fits in an int would come out right. But halving does not play well with the modulus: −1,794,917,296 / 2 is not half of the real product.
cards/3/wrong/2: By default C# does not check: the exception only comes inside checked.
cards/4/explain: x starts at n = nums.Length: index n has no slot in the array, so it goes in up front. The loop runs over indices 0..n − 1, so the condition is i < nums.Length. Each step brings both the index and the value into x: x ^= i ^ nums[i]. Without the indices (x ^= nums[i]) there is nothing to cancel against.
cards/5/task: Step through the trace on [9, 6, 4, 2, 3, 5, 7, 0, 1]: x collects the indices and values that have not met their pair yet. The rig asks twice what x becomes.
cards/5/goal/asks/0/q: x = 7. Step i = 5, nums[5] = 5. What does x become?
cards/5/goal/asks/0/explain: The index and the value are the same: i ^ nums[i] = 5 ^ 5 = 0, and x ^ 0 = x. The 5 arrived twice in one step and cancelled itself at once, so x stays 7.
cards/5/goal/asks/1/q: The last step: x = 1, i = 8, nums[8] = 1. What does x become?
cards/5/goal/asks/1/explain: x ^= 8 ^ 1. The 1 was already waiting in x — it came in as an index at i = 1 — and cancels. The 8 arrives for the first time, as an index, and will never arrive as a value: it is not in the array. x = 8. The 9 cancelled on the very first step: x started at n = 9, and nums[0] = 9.
cards/6/title: Single Number III: split the two singles by one bit
cards/6/body:
Single Number III (#260): exactly two numbers occur once, all the others occur twice. Return both, in O(n) time and O(1) memory. The XOR of the whole array gives x = a ^ b: the pairs cancelled, and the two singles got mixed together.

a ≠ b, so x ≠ 0, and every 1 in x is a bit where a and b differ. Take such a bit and split all numbers into two groups: those that have it and those that do not. a and b land in different groups, while both copies of any pair land in the same one — equal numbers have equal bits. The XOR of each group is one of the answers.

The lowest 1: x & −x. In two’s complement −x = ~x + 1 (the same as ~x == −x − 1). In ~x the trailing zeros of x became 1s; the +1 runs through them as a carry, clears them, and stops exactly at the position of the lowest 1 of x. Above it, −x equals ~x, the opposite of x. The AND keeps a single 1: 6 = 0110₂, −6 = …1010₂, 6 & −6 = 0010₂ = 2.
cards/7/task: Step through the trace on [1, 2, 1, 3, 2, 5]. The first pass folds the array into x = a ^ b, the second splits the numbers by one bit. The rig asks about that bit and about one group.
cards/7/goal/asks/0/explain: Compare 0110 and …1010 bit by bit. Bit 3 and up: x has zeros. Bit 2: x has a 1, −x a 0. Bit 1: both are 1. Bit 0: both are 0. Only one 1 in common, bit 1, so low = 2. x has bit 2 set as well, but −x has it cleared: x & −x keeps only the lowest 1.
cards/7/goal/asks/1/q: low = 2. The second pass has reached 3 = 011₂; right now a = 2, b = 0. What does the code do?
cards/7/goal/asks/1/explain: 3 & 2 = 2 ≠ 0 — the 3 has bit 1 set, so it goes to group a: 2 ^ 3 = 1. It is fine that a is not 3 yet: group a also holds the second 2, which comes next and cancels the first — then a becomes 3. The 5 (101₂) has bit 1 clear and goes to b.
cards/8/q: On [1, 2, 1, 3, 2, 5] this code returns [0, 6] instead of [3, 5]. Tap the line with the bug.
cards/8/explain: v & low is either 0 or low itself. Here low = 2, so v & low is 0 or 2 but never 1: every number goes to else, b = the XOR of the whole array = 6, a = 0. Compare with zero instead: (v & low) != 0. The same bug in a bit-k test: (x & (1 << k)) == 1 only works for k = 0.
cards/9/body:
Single Number II (#137): everything occurs three times, one number once. XOR will not do. Count each bit separately: how many numbers have it. The triples contribute a multiple of three, so count % 3 is the answer’s bit. O(32·n) time, O(1) memory; “everything k times” is solved the same way.

Set Mismatch (#645): the numbers 1..n, one is duplicated and another is missing. The XOR of 1..n and the array gives dup ^ miss — from there it is #260: split by the lowest 1, plus one more pass to tell which of the two is the duplicate.

The XOR swap a ^= b; b ^= a; a ^= b; is a party trick, not an optimisation: a plain swap through a temporary (or (a, b) = (b, a)) is no slower, and if a and b are the same slot (arr[i] and arr[j] with i == j), the XOR swap zeroes it.

In games the “undo = do it again” property gives Zobrist hashing: every (piece, square) pair gets a random 64-bit number, and the position hash is the XOR of the numbers of all pieces. A move updates the hash in O(1): XOR with the old square removes the piece, XOR with the new one places it. Turn-based game AIs use it to cache positions they have already evaluated, and networked games use it to compare client states.
cards/9/deep:
#137 without a loop over bits. Two counter words, ones and twos, keep for each bit the count modulo 3 (0, 1 or 2 — two bits of state): ones = (ones ^ v) & ~twos; twos = (twos ^ v) & ~ones;. After the pass, the answer is ones. It is a three-state machine applied to all 32 bits at once; O(n), but harder to explain in an interview than counting per bit.

x & −x on int.MinValue. If a ^ b = int.MinValue, −x wraps to the same int.MinValue, and x & −x = int.MinValue — the correct lowest 1 (bit 31). Inside checked, though, the negation throws OverflowException; write unchecked(x & -x) there.

Zobrist. Generate the table of random numbers once with a fixed seed — otherwise clients will not agree on hashes. Collisions happen: with 64 bits and a million positions the chance of at least one is about 3·10⁻⁸ by the birthday estimate (n² / 2⁶⁵), which is why transposition tables often store check bits next to the hash. string.GetHashCode will not do here — it is randomised per process.
cards/10/q: Which statements are true? Select all.
cards/10/options/1: In #260 any 1 bit of x would do instead of the lowest one
cards/10/options/2: The XOR swap is faster than a swap through a temporary
cards/10/options/3: Missing Number with a long sum and with XOR are both O(n) time and O(1) memory
cards/10/options/4: In #137 (everything three times) the XOR of the whole array is enough
cards/10/explain: 12 = 1100₂, its lowest 1 is bit 2, which is 4. Any 1 of x is a bit where a and b differ, so you can split by any of them; the lowest one is just the easiest to extract. The XOR swap is not faster and breaks on a single slot. Both Missing Number solutions are one pass and one variable. In #137 XOR leaves copies of the triples — you need the per-bit count.
cards/11/q: You are solving Single Number III out loud. Put the steps in order.
cards/11/items/0: Clarify: exactly two singles, every other number exactly twice; does the order of the answer matter
cards/11/items/1: Brute force: a dictionary of counts — O(n) time, but O(n) memory
cards/11/items/2: XOR of the whole array: pairs cancel, leaving x = a ^ b ≠ 0
cards/11/items/3: A bit where a and b differ: low = x & −x
cards/11/items/4: Second pass: XOR into two groups by (v & low) != 0
cards/11/items/6: Complexity: O(n) and O(1) memory; edge case — negative numbers
cards/11/explain: The problem, the dictionary baseline, then the two steps of the idea (fold with XOR, pick a bit), the second pass, a run and complexity. Negative numbers break nothing: both XOR and x & −x work in two’s complement.
cards/12/q: Match the condition to the technique.
cards/12/pairs/4/0: Position hash after a move in O(1)
